title: Technical SEO Migrations Need Executable Release Gates
seoTitle: Technical SEO Migrations: URL Maps and Release Gates
subtitle: Make every old URL’s outcome testable before moving the site.
seoDescription: Plan SEO migrations with a URL manifest, redirect-graph checks and page contracts. Test the public edge and separate implementation defects from index changes.

artwork.alt: A monochrome corridor of sequential checkpoints governs several converging release paths.
artwork.label: Migration controls / release corridor
artwork.caption: Redirects, canonicals, internal links, and release evidence must pass the same ordered checkpoints.

author: SULAYMAN BOWLES
thesis: Every important old URL needs an approved outcome, and every new canonical needs a page contract. Validate both through the delivered production stack, not only the new templates.

conclusion.title: Gate routing before declaring the move complete
conclusion.content: Require approved outcomes for important old URLs and passing page contracts for new routes through the public edge. Then monitor index consolidation, crawling, and performance separately; passing publisher-controlled checks cannot guarantee their timing or results.

evidenceBoundary: Passing migration gates proves the tested publisher-controlled routing and page signals. It cannot guarantee unchanged rankings, traffic, crawling cadence, index consolidation, or behavior in untested caches, regions, clients, and external systems.

sources.label: Google Search: site moves and URL migrations

Google Crawling Infrastructure: HTTP status codes

content: A new site can look finished while old links lead nowhere. Users, crawlers, analytics, caches, and indexes still address the previous system. Visual review cannot prove that redirects preserve intent, retired routes left navigation, canonicals agree with sitemaps, or rendered content survived.

Inventory meaningful old URLs and give each an approved outcome. Generate routing and metadata from that map, validate the build, capture the real production responses, and monitor traffic alongside coverage gaps. Critical route classes must converge before release; accepted exceptions need owners and expiry.

sections.title: Build an attributed URL inventory
paragraphs: Merge sitemaps, crawls, logs, analytics landings, Search Console exports, backlinks, CMS or database routes, feeds, campaigns, and known files. Each misses something. Preserve the source and latest meaningful activity for every URL so omissions remain visible.

Assign keep, equivalent move, reviewed merge, terminal not-found or gone, temporary retention with sunset, or non-public/invalid exclusion. Redirecting everything to home is not a mapping; it leaves product decisions unresolved and sends users to poor destinations.

Record content type, locale, template, indexability, canonical, redirect status, priority, owner, validation contract, and exception rationale. Prevent multiple outcomes for one old URL and accidental ownership of one route by several new pages. Review changes because this manifest drives public behavior.

table.caption: Migration URL-manifest fields
rows: Keep, move, merge, remove, temporary, exclude

sections.title: Compile and test the route contracts
paragraphs: Generate routes, redirects, canonicals, sitemaps, links, and where possible analytics mappings from the manifest. Reject route collisions, redirect cycles, relative canonicals, staging hosts, malformed URLs, noindex sitemap entries, and links still targeting retired routes.

Build and parse priority templates. Check main heading, canonical, directives, meaningful visible content, status behavior, schema agreement, and navigation. Compare JavaScript source with a pinned browser render using page-specific completion conditions. Screenshots supplement these checks; they do not establish routing.

Check critical and high-traffic URLs completely. Stratify long-tail coverage by template, locale, disposition, depth, query behavior, and source. Retain the full manifest denominator and explicitly report untested rows.
bullets: Fail on unmapped priority URLs and duplicate old-route ownership.
Fail on redirect loops, chains beyond policy, and destinations that do not exist.
Fail on staging, preview, localhost, or alternate-host canonicals.
Fail on canonical sitemap rows that redirect, noindex, or canonicalize elsewhere.
Fail when required visible content or structured data disappears from a template.
Report untested manifest rows as coverage gaps.

sections.title: Resolve every move to its approved destination
paragraphs: For lasting moves, permanent server redirects are the clearest option; Google documents 301 and 308 as permanent signals. Select by method semantics and platform support, testing actual methods when non-GET requests matter. Redirect codes do not all transform requests identically.

Resolve the map before deployment, aiming for one hop from each moved URL to its exact approved destination. Fold historical aliases into the new mapping instead of chaining through old routes. Reject cycles, competing destinations, and targets that redirect again.

When no equivalent exists, 404 or 410 can express removal more honestly than a blanket category or homepage redirect. Product owners decide equivalence; string similarity may suggest candidates but must not silently merge user intent.

table.caption: Redirect-graph validation
rows: One permanent hop to approved equivalent
Redirect ends at error, noindex, or another redirect

sections.title: Keep the launch and baseline attributable
paragraphs: Freeze the manifest and record application, edge, redirect, sitemap, and analytics versions. Capture old responses, priority templates, internal graph, sitemap counts, and relevant traffic before launch. This baseline separates expected movement from breakage; it does not promise stable metrics.

Coordinate routing and pages so old URLs never lose their intended outcome. Purge or version caches deliberately. Fetch public-host smoke routes from outside the origin network to exercise CDN rules, platform redirects, TLS, host normalization, and middleware.

Where supported, limit canary routes or traffic in a way meaningful for public URLs and crawlers. Define rollback triggers for 5xx spikes, loops, content loss, canonical-host corruption, analytics loss, and critical transaction failures. Restore a coherent route set, not just the frontend.

codeExamples.title: Redirect checks
codeExamples.description: Run against a reviewed manifest sample and save headers and bodies as launch evidence.
codeExamples.code:
curl -sS -D old.headers -o /dev/null https://old.example.com/priority-page
curl -sS -L --max-redirs 5 -D chain.headers \
  -o final.html https://old.example.com/priority-page

rg -o '<link[^>]+rel="canonical"[^>]+>' final.html
rg -o '<meta[^>]+name="robots"[^>]+>' final.html

sections.title: Separate implementation defects from index transition
paragraphs: Monitor old and new route responses, redirects, 404 and 410 volume, server errors, latency, canonical conflicts, sitemap fetches, retired-link references, render failures, analytics continuity, and conversion paths. These implementation signals have short feedback loops.

Crawler requests, indexed examples, submitted versus discovered sitemap states, selected canonicals, impressions, clicks, and landing-page shifts follow external timelines. Google notes moves take time and crawl frequency varies. Report dates and denominators; traffic movement alone does not establish a routing defect.

Link incidents to manifest rows, production captures, owners, decisions, repairs, and validating reruns. Retain redirects for users and systems still using old URLs, applying provider guidance and product constraints when reviewing their removal. The end of a launch window is not a removal rule.
